newsitem.title: USA: U.S. envoy pushes Iraq Kurds for ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy pushes Iraq Kurds for ceasefire.

text.p: A senior U.S. diplomat met Iraqi Kurdish warlord Massoud Barzani in Turkey on Monday for talks on ending Kurdish clashes that have damaged Washington's influence in north Iraq.
Envoy Robert Pelletreau said Barzani looked positively on a U.S.-proposed ceasefire with his rival Jalal Talabani to "permit stability in the area for establishing an end to the fighting".
Pelletreau, assistant secretary of state for near eastern affairs, warned against any military involvement by Iran or Iraq in the fighting.

"The United States would regard that as a negative development that could have very negative consequences," he told reporters after meeting Barzani for more than three hours at a Turkish military base in the border town of Silopi.

Fighting between the two factions since August has raised the profile of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein in northern Iraq and effectively ended the U.S. military, aid and intelligence presence in the mountainous Kurdish region.
Barzani tipped the balance of power in his favour in late August by joining with Iraqi troops and tanks to take Arbil, Iraqi Kurdistan's former administrative centre.
This alliance led to U.S. missile strikes on military installations in southern Iraq in reprisal but Barzani has threatened to call on Baghdad for help again if pressed too hard in the field.
Barzani's Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) accuses Talabani's Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) of receiving military aid from Iran. Tehran and Talabani deny the charge.
Pelletreau said he would have a better idea of how the U.S. peace bid was going after a meeting with Talabani set for Tuesday in Ankara.
"Obviously agreement requires agreement of more than one party," Pelletreau said.
It was unclear how Talabani would get to Turkey for the talks. Barzani controls most of the Iraqi side of the Turkish border.
"We are trying to finalize Mr Talabani's travelling arrangements," Turkish foreign ministry spokesman Sermet Atatcanli said.
The rival Kurdish groups exchanged artillery fire for control of the strategic Dukan Dam for the second day running on Monday, witnesses said.

Forces loyal to Barzani were attempting to take the dam and push on to the city of Sulaimaniya, the PUK's stronghold. Control of the city, northern Iraq' biggest, would give Barzani a strong card to play at the negotating table.
The Kurds broke from Baghdad at the end of the 1991 Gulf War and set up a power-sharing parliament in Arbil that collapsed in December 1994 when Talabani's forces took control of the city.
Fighting that continued sporadically after that was over control of Arbil and the distribution of revenues from the KDP's makeshift oil trade across the Turkish border.
Washington brokered two meetings in Ireland last year between the Kurdish factions but no solid settlement was reached.
